newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission says competitive performance "poor".
newsitem.headline: EU Commission says competitive performance "poor".

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday painted a largely negative picture of the continent's competitive power, saying the EU was lagging behind rival economic superpowers the United States and Japan in key areas.
The EU's executive said that while there were several areas of strength in the European economy, the competitive performance of industry was poor.

"The European Union is not exploiting its full potential or meeting the performance of its major competitors in terms of living standards, productivity and employment creation, leading to idle resources and high rates of unemployment," it said in an analysis.
As a result, the EU level of gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is nearly one third below that of the United States and one sixth below that of Japan.
"Such a result is by no means inevitable and should not be considered as acceptable," said the report due to be presented to the Commission on Wednesday.

High costs and low investment have combined to depress Europe's industrial performance, it said. Public deficits are too high, spending on research insufficient and the adoption of new technologies remain too slow.
In spite of much improved economic fundamentals, European industry has not been performing as well as it might.
"In most manufacturing sectors, the United States continued to lead European productivity," the Commission report said.

The share of the 15-nation EU -- grouping the most developed industrial countries in Europe -- in export markets in the 28-nation Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development has been declining since 1987.

Europe, struggling with near-record levels of joblessness, continues to lag significantly behind the United States in both labour productivity and the employment rate -- the share of the working age population in work, the Commission added.
Since 1960, the EU has mananged to create only 10 million new jobs net, half the number generated in Japan and less than a fifth of those in the United States.
As a result, the EU unemployment rate stands at almost 11 percent of the workforce, twice as high as in the United States and three times more than in Japan.
Over the last 10 years, the report said, industrial value added rose by less than in both the United States and Japan.
"Of the manufacturing sectors, only food, drink, and tobacco and wood and furniture grew faster in the European Union than in the United States and Japan between 1985 and 1995," the Commission said.
Also on the negative side, the report noted that EU prices for key service inputs like communications, transport and financial and business services were higher than elsewhere.
In addition, long-term interest rates are above those in the United States and Japan, making it more costly for firms to raise loans.
